messages.subject: Binomial count data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I use point transect to estimate densities of songbirds. I have grouped
the data into binomial count data (birds occuring within 30 meters and
birds occuring outside 30 meters) as in Bibby et al. 1985. As I run the
analysis, I get the message "the number of intervals are less than the
number of key parameters" How do I treat binomial counts in Distance
3.5?

Vera Hausner

messages.subject: Re: Binomial count data
messages.body_plain:
> > I use point transect to estimate densities of songbirds. I have grouped
> > the data into binomial count data (birds occuring within 30 meters and
> > birds occuring outside 30 meters) as in Bibby et al. 1985. As I run the
> > analysis, I get the message "the number of intervals are less than the
> > number of key parameters" How do I treat binomial counts in Distance
> > 3.5?

You can only fit one parameter models to binomial data.  Thus you could
fit the half-normal key with no adjustments (recommended), or the uniform
key with one adjustment.  You cannot fit the hazard-rate model using
DISTANCE.  Alternatively, you can fit the half-normal model using the
equation given for binomial data in the distance sampling book (see
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/ ).

Steve Buckland

Francisco,
My reply won't help you with the = basic question=20 that you asked, but adds something else for you to consider.  =
 
It is quite possible that roads may effect rabbits = in some=20 way.  Many species have some response to roads even if it is = minor. =20 Usually the vegetation adjacent to roads is different (or at least = somewhat=20 altered) from the vegetation of the surrounding landscape.  This = difference=20 in vegetation can create habitat differences and effect the population = of=20 rabbits adjacent to roads.  You may introduce considerable bias if = you use=20 roads for your line transects.  You might want to read a paper that = is in=20 final draft for publication in Conservation Biology:  The Ecological Effects of Roads on Terrestrial and Aquatic=20 Communities: A Review , by Stephen C. Trombulak and Christopher A.=20 Frissell.  You might be able to get a copy from Chris Frissell (fris...@selway.umt.edu).
 
I realize that roads may be your best = way of=20 accessing the area, but you might want to do some sampling away from = roads to=20 reduce the bias.

messages.subject: comparing distance results
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I have analysed results of a census of Colobus monkeys using Distance
(cheers Len).I would like to compare the results I have for 3 line
transects. Each transect was sampled repaetedly over a period of two weeks.
However the "effort" is different for one: 34.5,compared with 33 and 33. The
number of observations vary: 63,48,54. When I analyse them separately
Distance selects the uniform/cosine model for two and the halfnormal/hermite
for one.  I would like to be able to compare the densities of the three to
see if there is a significant difference and to relate any difference to
vegetation type. Is there a simple way to compare the three results?
If you are able to offer any suggestions please reply to:
darr...@hotmail.com
Many thanks,
Darren Norris

messages.subject: Distance 3.5 Install problems
messages.body_plain:
To Distance 3.5 users:

Has anyone experienced the following problem?

- You install Distance 3.5 apparently without problems
- When you come to run it, you get
   Run-time error '91'
   Object variable or With block variable not set

If so, please contact me (dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk).  Two people so far have
reported this problem to me, but I can't reproduce it on any of our machines
here, so I don't know how to go about fixing it.

Thanks,

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland
